**Solution 2 is the one I'd trust, though I checked it by reasoning rather than against the source paper.**

**Solution 2's construction checks out.** Take a balanced blow-up of $C_5$. It is triangle-free, since every triangle would need an odd closed walk of length 3 in $C_5$. Colour each edge between consecutive classes by the colour of its head vertex, with each vertex having a private colour. Every 4-cycle in the blow-up maps to a closed walk of length 4 in $C_5$, which must backtrack, so it reuses a colour. Each vertex sees $\lfloor n/5\rfloor$ distinct out-neighbour colours plus its own colour on incoming edges, so $\delta^c = \lfloor n/5\rfloor + 1$ with no rainbow $C_4$.

**The threshold is tight for every residue.** Writing $\lceil (n+6)/5\rceil - 1$ for the largest value of $\delta^c$ that fails to force a rainbow $C_4$, one gets $\lfloor n/5\rfloor + 1$ in each residue class mod 5. So $(n+6)/5$ is exactly one step above this construction for all $n$. A smaller offset such as $(n+5)/5$ would be refuted by the same construction when $n \equiv 0 \pmod 5$.

**Solution 1 is unsupported.** $(n+1)/3$ would need a triangle-free construction with minimum colour degree near $n/3$ and no rainbow $C_4$. I know of none, and the $C_5$ construction only reaches about $n/5$.

**Solution 3 is invalid.** Its host graph joins $V_1, V_2, V_3$ cyclically, which is a complete tripartite graph and contains triangles. It is therefore not triangle-free, so its lower-bound construction does not apply.

The upper bound $(n+6)/5$ rests on my recollection of a published result (I could not verify it here), so my confidence is moderate rather than certain.

CHOICE: 2
